lead: This unit is about limits: which problems a Turing machine can always answer, which it can only half answer, and what the answer costs in time and space. After it you can prove a problem undecidable by reduction, use Rice's theorem and Post's correspondence problem, and place a language in P, NP, NP-complete or NP-hard.
about: Unit 6 draws the line between problems a computer can solve and problems it cannot, then measures the cost of the ones it can. Chapter 6.1 splits languages into recursive and recursively enumerable by how a Turing machine is allowed to halt. Chapter 6.2 turns that split into a working test for decidability, and 6.3 proves the halting problem undecidable by diagonalization. Chapter 6.4 generalizes that proof with Rice's theorem, and 6.5 adds Post's correspondence problem, an undecidable puzzle with no machines in sight. Chapter 6.6 ties the results back to computable functions. Chapter 6.7 starts counting steps and tape cells, and 6.8 collects languages into the classes P and NP and names the NP-complete problems at the top of NP.

chapters.idea: A language is recursive when some Turing machine always halts and answers correctly, and recursively enumerable when some machine accepts exactly its strings but may loop on the rest.
chapters.depth: Define both classes through halting behaviour only. Recursive is also called decidable or Turing-decidable; recursively enumerable (r.e.) is also called recognizable, semi-decidable or Turing-acceptable. State the chain recursive ⊂ r.e. ⊂ all languages. Cover closure: recursive languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation and Kleene star; r.e. languages are closed under union and intersection but not complement. Prove the key theorem: L is recursive if and only if L and its complement are both r.e. Mention enumerators: L is r.e. exactly when some machine lists its strings one by one.

figure.aria: Three nested sets: recursive languages inside r.e. languages inside all languages, with the halting language in the middle ring.
figure.caption: Decidable languages form the innermost set; the halting language is r.e. while its complement is not r.e. at all.

chapters.example: Question: L and its complement are both r.e. Show that L is decidable. Let machine M accept L and machine M′ accept the complement of L. Build a decider D. On input w = 0110, D runs M on 0110 for 1 step, then M′ on 0110 for 1 step, then M for 2 steps, then M′ for 2 steps, and so on. Since 0110 lies in exactly one of the two languages, one machine accepts it after some s steps. D reaches that round after at most s² simulated steps plus a constant of bookkeeping, so D always halts. D answers yes if M accepted and no if M′ accepted.
chapters.trap: Assuming an r.e. language must halt on every input, or that r.e. is closed under complement. r.e. guarantees halting only on the strings inside the language.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5: Turing machine model, instantaneous descriptions, language acceptance, universal Turing machine.
chapters.leave: Reductions and undecidability proofs go to 6.2 and 6.3; machine design stays in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A problem is decidable when some Turing machine halts on every input with the correct yes or no, and undecidable when no such machine can exist.
chapters.depth: Turn problems into languages over an alphabet by encoding objects, writing ⟨M⟩ for the code of a machine and ⟨M,w⟩ for a machine with an input. Distinguish decidable, undecidable and partially solvable (r.e. but not recursive) problems. List decidable samples quickly, leaning on earlier units: membership, emptiness, finiteness and equivalence for DFA and for CFG. List undecidable samples: whether M accepts w, whether L(M) is empty, whether two machines accept the same language, whether M ever prints a stated symbol. Teach many-one (mapping) reductions: A ≤m B when a computable f gives x ∈ A ⟺ f(x) ∈ B; then B decidable implies A decidable, and A undecidable implies B undecidable. Some syllabi call this reducibility.

figure.title: Mapping reduction A ≤m B
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain: an instance of A becomes an instance of B through a computable map, and B's decider answers A.
figure.caption: Undecidability travels backwards along the chain: if A has no decider, B cannot have one either.

chapters.example: Question: show that the language {⟨M⟩ : M accepts the string 101} is undecidable. Take any machine M and word w. Build a new machine M′ that works like this: on input x, if x is not 101, reject at once; if x is 101, simulate M on w and accept exactly when M accepts w. Then M′ accepts 101 if and only if M accepts w. A decider for our language would decide whether M accepts w, which is undecidable, so our language is undecidable too.
chapters.trap: Saying 'no algorithm is known' instead of giving a reduction. Also reversing the arrow: to prove B undecidable you reduce a known undecidable A to B, never B to A.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for recursive versus r.e.; Unit 2 and Unit 3 for the decidable examples.
chapters.leave: The diagonalization proof is 6.3, Rice's theorem is 6.4, Post's correspondence problem is 6.5, and polynomial-time reductions are 6.8.

chapters.idea: No Turing machine can decide, for every machine M and input w, whether M eventually halts on w.
chapters.depth: State HALT = {⟨M,w⟩ : M halts on w} and A_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w}, both undecidable. Prove undecidability by diagonalization: assume a decider H, build D that loops when H says halts and halts when H says loops, then run D on its own code. Show HALT is r.e. (simulate M on w) but not recursive, and its complement is not r.e. Cover the close variants: halting on the empty input, halting on every input, and halting on its own code. Draw the practical consequence: no general loop checker or full program verifier exists, even though the universal machine of Unit 5 can run any program. Some syllabi write the pair as (M, w) coded in binary over {0,1}.

figure.title: Halting behaviour and the flipped diagonal
figure.aria: A four by four table of yes and no answers, with the main diagonal marked, showing where each machine is questioned about its own code.
figure.caption: Columns are the codes of M1 to M4, rows are the machines. The machine D answers opposite to each marked diagonal entry, so D behaves like no row in the table.

chapters.example: Question: prove the halting problem undecidable. Assume H decides it: H(⟨M,w⟩) = yes when M halts on w and no otherwise. The table gives four machines questioned about each other's codes; the marked diagonal holds yes, no, no, yes. Build D: on input ⟨M⟩, run H on ⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩, loop forever if H answers yes, and halt if H answers no. So D answers no, yes, yes, no on the four codes and differs from every row. Now feed D its own code: D halts on ⟨D⟩ only if H says D loops on ⟨D⟩, which happens only if D loops on ⟨D⟩. Both cases contradict, so H cannot exist.
chapters.trap: Thinking 'just run M on w' decides halting: if M has not stopped after a long time you still cannot say no. Also do not mix up the assumed machine H with the constructed machine D.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 for recursive versus r.e.; 6.2 for the meaning of a decision problem; Unit 5 for the universal machine.
chapters.leave: Rice's theorem generalizes this proof in 6.4; the running time of the simulation appears in 6.7.

chapters.idea: Every nontrivial property of the language a Turing machine accepts is undecidable.
chapters.depth: Say what a property is here: a set P of r.e. languages. P is trivial when P is empty or holds for every r.e. language. Rice's theorem: for nontrivial P, the language {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ∈ P} is undecidable. Give the proof by reduction from A_TM: pick a machine M₁ whose language is in P and a machine M₂ whose language is not, then from ⟨M,w⟩ build M′ that runs M on w first and afterwards behaves like M₁ if M halted and like M₂ if it did not. Stress that the theorem speaks about semantic properties of L(M), not syntactic properties of the code such as number of states or whether the head ever moves left, which may well be decidable. Consequences: emptiness, finiteness, regularity, context-freeness and 'L(M) = Σ*' are all undecidable. The theorem does not claim the set is unrecognizable; many of these sets are r.e. Some syllabi state it as Rice's theorem for index sets.

figure.title: Rice's theorem by reduction
figure.aria: A downward flow from assuming the property decidable, building M-prime from a halting instance, to the two possible languages it accepts and the resulting contradiction.
figure.caption: Whether M halts on w decides which of L₁ and L₂ the new machine accepts, so a decider for P would decide halting.

chapters.example: Question: use Rice's theorem to show that {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is finite} is undecidable. Let P be the set of finite r.e. languages. P is nontrivial: the empty language is finite and Σ* is infinite, and both are r.e. Take any ⟨M,w⟩ and build M′: on input x, simulate M on w and accept x if that simulation halts. If M halts on w then M′ accepts every x, so L(M′) = Σ*, which is infinite. If M never halts on w then M′ accepts nothing, so L(M′) = ∅, which is finite. A decider for finiteness would then tell us whether M halts on w. Therefore finiteness is undecidable.
chapters.trap: Applying Rice to the machine text, as in 'M has three states' or 'M halts within 100 steps', which are decidable. Also forgetting the one-line proof that the property is nontrivial.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for reductions; 6.3 for the halting problem used in the proof.
chapters.leave: Post's correspondence problem is a separate undecidable problem in 6.5; complexity classes start at 6.7.

chapters.idea: Deciding whether a finite set of domino pairs can be arranged so that the top string equals the bottom string is undecidable, and so is the version that fixes the first domino.
chapters.depth: Define a PCP instance: two lists A = w₁…wₖ and B = x₁…xₖ of nonempty strings over an alphabet Σ, written as dominoes (wᵢ on top, xᵢ below). A match is a sequence of indices i₁…iₘ with w_{i₁}…w_{iₘ} = x_{i₁}…x_{iₘ}. PCP asks whether a match exists and is undecidable. The modified PCP (MPCP) demands i₁ = 1 and is also undecidable. Explain the proof outline: reduce the acceptance problem for Turing machines to MPCP by encoding configurations as domino strings, then reduce MPCP to PCP by adding a new symbol ♯ that only the first domino can carry, forcing a match to start at domino 1, plus a closing domino that ends the match. Keep the encoding construction at outline level and spend time on the definition, the two versions and why the extra first-domino rule makes MPCP the easier stepping stone.

figure.title: Three dominoes, top list A and bottom list B
figure.aria: A two-row table of three dominoes, with the top strings and bottom strings of each domino in the same numbered column.
figure.caption: Taking dominoes 1, 2, 3 gives top a·ab·bab and bottom aab·b·ab, and both strings are aabbab.

chapters.example: Question: over Σ = {a,b} the dominoes are 1 = (a, aab), 2 = (ab, b) and 3 = (bab, ab). Find a match. Take the sequence 1, 2, 3. The top strings join to a·ab·bab = aabbab, and the bottom strings join to aab·b·ab = aabbab. The strings are equal, so 1, 2, 3 is a match. It also begins with domino 1, so the same sequence is a valid MPCP solution. No single domino matches itself, and the short tries fail: 1,2 gives aab against aabb, 1,3 gives abab against aabab, 2,3 gives abbab against bab.
chapters.trap: Greedily extending a partial match as if it were progress: a partial arrangement proves nothing until the two strings are exactly equal. Also keep PCP and MPCP apart, since MPCP forces the first domino to be used first.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 for reductions; 6.3 for the halting problem that the full proof reduces from.
chapters.leave: The complete domino encoding of Turing machine moves is sketched only; complexity versions of PCP are not needed here.

chapters.idea: A function is computable when a Turing machine halts on every input with the right output on its tape, and partial computable when it is allowed to loop on some inputs.
chapters.depth: Define computable (total, Turing-computable) and partial computable functions from Σ* to Σ*. Cover encodings and Gödel-style numbering of machines, pairs and grammars, written ⟨M⟩ and ⟨M,w⟩. Define the characteristic function χ_L with value 1 on strings of L and 0 outside, and prove L decidable if and only if χ_L is computable. Prove L r.e. if and only if L is the domain of a partial computable function, equivalently the range of a computable function. Note that composition of computable functions is computable and that total functions are a strict subset of the partial ones. Some syllabi continue into recursive function theory with primitive recursion and μ-recursion; name these only.

figure.title: Total and partial computable functions
figure.aria: A downward flow from an input to a machine, branching into a halting branch that outputs f of x and a looping branch where the value is undefined.
figure.caption: When the halting branch always happens the function is total; the looping branch is allowed only for partial functions.

chapters.example: Question: show that f(x) = x + 1 in unary is computable and that the halting function is only partial computable. A unary number n is the string aⁿ. On input aaa (n = 3) the machine walks right over the three a's, reaches the blank in cell 4, writes a there, and halts with aaaa, so f(aaa) = aaaa. It does this for every input, so f is total and computable. Now set g(M,w) = 1 when M halts on w, and leave g undefined otherwise. A machine that simulates M on w and writes 1 only if the simulation stops computes g, so g is partial computable. If g were total computable, halting would be decidable; it is not, so g is not total computable.
chapters.trap: Assuming every r.e. language has a computable characteristic function, when only the recursive ones do, and treating a partial function as if it had a value at every input.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for the machine model; 6.1 for decidable versus r.e.; 6.3 for the halting problem.
chapters.leave: Recursive function theory details such as primitive recursion and μ-recursion stay as names; cost of computation starts in 6.7.

chapters.idea: The cost of a Turing machine is measured as a function of the input length n: time is the number of steps and space is the number of tape cells used, both in the worst case.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter in detail. Define running time t(n) as the maximum number of steps of M over all inputs of length n, and space s(n) as the maximum number of distinct cells scanned. Insist on worst case and on asymptotic notation O and Θ. Define the classes TIME(t(n)) and SPACE(s(n)). Explain why a read-only input tape is used so that space below n can be discussed, and why on a single tape the input cells count, giving space at least n. Quote the useful bounds: a machine running in time t(n) with t(n) ≥ n uses at most t(n) + 1 cells, TIME(f) ⊆ SPACE(f) for f(n) ≥ n, and SPACE(s) ⊆ TIME(2^{O(s)}) for s(n) ≥ log₂ n. State the time and space hierarchy theorems in one line: with more time or space, strictly more languages are decidable for reasonable constructible bounds.

figure.aria: Three curves rising with input length: a straight line for n, a slightly higher curve for n log-two n, and a much steeper parabola for n squared.
figure.caption: At n = 20 the linear machine needs 20 steps, the quadratic one 400, so the gap grows quickly with input length.

chapters.example: Question: compare the time used by two machines on an input of length n = 6, the word 000111. Machine M₁ only scans to the end and checks that the last two symbols are 1s: it makes n + 1 = 7 steps, so M₁ runs in TIME(n). Machine M₂ decides {0ᵏ1ᵏ} by crossing out one 0 and one 1 per round. Each round scans at most 2n = 12 cells, and there are k = 3 rounds, so M₂ uses at most n² = 36 steps on this input and in general runs in TIME(n²). M₂ also uses at most 6 cells, which here equals the input length.
chapters.trap: Measuring cost against the value written in the input rather than its length: a number near 2ⁿ in binary has length only n. Also forgetting that on a single tape the input cells count as space.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 for tapes, heads and multitape machines; 6.1 for decidable languages.
chapters.leave: P, NP and completeness are 6.8; hierarchy theorem proofs are quoted, not proved.

chapters.idea: P holds the languages decided in polynomial time, NP holds the languages with short certificates checked in polynomial time, and the NP-complete languages are the hardest ones inside NP.
chapters.depth: Define TIME(nᵏ) and P as their union. Define NP by certificates: x is in L when some string y with |y| ≤ p(|x|) makes a polynomial-time verifier V accept the pair (x,y); state that this equals acceptance by a polynomial-time nondeterministic machine. Define polynomial-time many-one reduction ≤p, then NP-hard (every NP language reduces to it) and NP-complete (NP-hard and in NP). State the Cook–Levin theorem: SAT, and hence 3SAT, is NP-complete. Sketch the standard chain SAT ≤p 3SAT ≤p CLIQUE ≤p VERTEX-COVER, with SUBSET-SUM and HAMILTONIAN CYCLE as further NP-complete problems. Note that P = NP is open, that NP-hard problems may lie outside NP, and name co-NP and PSPACE briefly.

figure.aria: Three nested sets with P innermost, NP around it and PSPACE outermost, holding one or more named problems in each ring.
figure.caption: Every P problem is in NP and every NP problem is in PSPACE; nobody knows whether the two inner containments are strict.

chapters.example: Question: show that HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is in NP, using the graph on vertices 1 to 5 with edges 12, 23, 34, 45, 51, 13 and 24. A yes-instance must carry a certificate, here the sequence of vertices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The verifier checks that the 5 vertices are distinct, that 12, 23, 34 and 45 are edges, and that 51 closes the cycle, then accepts. That is 5 edge lookups and 5 comparisons, work of order n² with n = 5, so a certificate is checked in polynomial time and the language lies in NP. It is also NP-complete, so a polynomial-time decider for it would prove P = NP.
chapters.trap: Reading NP as 'not polynomial'. NP-hard problems need not be in NP, and to prove B NP-hard you reduce a known NP-hard problem to B, not the other way round. Certificates exist only for yes-instances.
chapters.prereq: 6.7 for TIME and SPACE classes; 6.2 for the idea of a reduction.
chapters.leave: Full reduction constructions, approximation algorithms and PSPACE-completeness proofs belong to later courses.
